text.p: Following are the main stories in Croatian newspapers on Wednesday.
- State-owned oil company INA gives up stakes in non-oil businesses. Its debts taken over by the bank rehabilitation agency.
- Croatia's workforce shrank 0.34 percent in January to 1.43 million with only a mild increase in housing and utilities branches and small enterprises.

- Loss-making metal industry Djuro Djakovic plans to invest 55 million German marks in its production facilities this year, says director A. Milovic. Output higher in 1996 and 1997 begins with new orders for Croatian and foreign markets.
- Croatian insurers blame government for failing to legalise tax relief that would encourage people taking out more insurance policies.
Life insurance represented a meagre 7.0 percent of all policies in 1996, compared with some 20 percent in transitional economies and up to 70 percent in the developed countries.

- Croatia ranks 22nd for corruption on a list of 42 countries, according to an independent survey. This should be combatted by legal measures, but the best weapon against corruption is to end economic stagnation, says law professor Josip Kregar.
- Researcher City Trust sees industrial output decline slowing down to only 0.4 percent in March.
- Stock market: Food concern Podravka and Adriatic pipeline operator JANAF stood out as fastest-growing stocks last week.
- The U.S. State Department human rights report includes serious accusations of media suppression in Croatia.
- Serb leaders interrupt cooperation on reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. Local Serb politicians in Eastern Slavonia fell prey to their own unrealistic demands, says government official Ivica Vrkic.

- Commentary by economist Z. Rohatinski: Croatia's economy still dominated by consumption and not production and export growth. Despite partial peacetime progress, industry still slow in recovering. -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
